title: Non-lossy interop translator for OpenAI Responses compatibility
creator: Maya Thompson
description:
Summary: Implement a translator layer that converts between Redwood's native response envelope and the OpenAI Responses API event model without dropping semantics needed for tooling, streaming, or structured outputs. Goal is deterministic, reversible translation where possible, and explicit lossiness documentation where not.

Background: Multiple product teams need a compatibility mode so customers using OpenAI Responses SDKs can switch to Redwood hosted/dedicated/private runtimes with minimal code changes. Prior adapters had subtle behavior differences around partial stream events, tool call handoffs, and schema-anchored structured outputs which caused regressions in downstream evals.

Scope:
- Design an interop translator that operates at the runtime ingress/egress boundary and preserves: streaming chunk boundaries, function/tool invocation call lifecycle, and structured-output anchors (schema IDs, typed fields).
- Provide a lossiness detector that emits a labeled diagnostic when exact round-trip fidelity cannot be guaranteed (e.g., OpenAI event omitted metadata we rely on).
- Add transformation rules for: chunked token events, delta vs full content patches, toolcall start/finish/error events, and structured-output scaffolding (json_schema -> Redwood type hints).
- Expose opt-in strict/lenient modes for clients: strict mode fails on lossy translation; lenient mode emits warnings and attempts graceful mapping.

Key design decisions and trade-offs:
1) Envelope vs event mapping: We will keep the native Redwood envelope internally and translate to the OpenAI event stream on egress. This avoids pervasive runtime changes but adds per-request translation CPU cost. Trade-off: slightly higher p50 for small responses, offset by memoized translation for hot paths.
2) Streaming chunk semantics: Preserve original chunk boundaries where possible; when differences arise (tokenization or kernel-driven chunking), add a synthetic "chunk_boundary_hint" field in the translated event to help SDKs reassemble. This is an extensible signal and avoids altering the primary text payload.
3) Tool/function calling lifecycle: Map Redwood's internal tool invocation lifecycle into OpenAI-style events: tool_call_started, tool_call_stream, tool_call_completed, tool_call_error. To avoid losing intermediate metadata, include a compact base64-encoded metadata blob in a reserved event field if the exact structure diverges.
4) Structured outputs: Use schema anchoring (schema_id + path) when translating and carry a checksum of the original object to enable downstream detectors to validate equivalence. If a schema cannot be represented in OpenAI's shape, mark as lossy and include a machine-readable reason.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for each mapping rule (100+ cases).
- An E2E harness that runs existing OpenAI-based client test suites against Redwood using the translator in both strict and lenient modes.
- Canary plan: start with internal canary on runtime-qa, then select customer beta with feature flag. Monitor: translation_loss_rate, stream_reassembly_errors, toolcall_mismatch_rate, p50/p95 latency delta.

Canary & rollout plan:
- Stage 1 (runtime-qa): translator off by default, smoke tests only.
- Stage 2 (internal beta): opt-in flag for specific orgs; observe metrics for 72h.
- Stage 3 (customer beta): 5 customers with documented use-cases.
- Stage 4 (GA): enabled by default in compatibility mode, opt-out available.

Operational runbooks:
- If translation_loss_rate > 0.5% for 1h, auto-disable strict mode and notify platform on-call.
- If stream_reassembly_errors spike, capture trace and a payload dump; run diagnostic tool to compute chunk boundary deltas.

Artifacts & links:
- Technical spec: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RESP/Non-lossy+Interop+Translator
- Design diagrams: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/interop-translator-design
- PoC repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4821
- Test harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/interop-tests/tree/translator-e2e

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should we expose the chunk_boundary_hint to external SDKs or keep it strictly internal? PM prefers external for observability, but security wants minimal surface area.
- Can we reuse existing KV cache keys for translation memoization or do we need a separate small cache?
- Define SLA/latency targets for translator overhead to determine whether A/B rollout to latency-sensitive routes is allowed.

Acceptance criteria:
- Translation preserves token ordering and toolcall lifecycle for >= 99.5% of test cases in strict mode.
- Lossiness diagnostics are generated and surfaced to the Console with actionable metadata.
- Canary completes without high-severity customer regressions and meets latency SLOs for 95% of routes.
comments: 2026-02-16: Kickoff sync with PM and Design. Agreed to anchor on schema_id for structured outputs (Maya).
2026-02-20: Spike complete. Proved chunk_boundary_hint reduces reassembly errors in SDK sim by 78% (Rohit). Link to perf notes: https://docs.redwood.ai/notes/translator-spike-2026-02-20
2026-02-28: Architecture review with Runtime team. Decided to keep translator at ingress/egress layer to minimize runtime churn (approved by Diego).
2026-03-03: Security review flagged the metadata blob as potential sensitive leak; added a stripping step for customer secrets and an allowlist (team security).

2026-03-08: Internal QA run found a regression for multi-tool sessions where concurrent tool_call_stream events interleave. Mitigation: attach monotonic session IDs and ordering counters. Working on patch (Rohit).
2026-03-10: PM review: requested opt-in UX copy and Console instrumentation to show translation warnings. Added follow-up PM ticket (PM-4082).
